messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Khalil's Silence

Khalil was seventy-eight when the accident happened, though in the months that followed he sometimes felt as though he had aged a decade in a single afternoon. He had spent fifty-two years as an environmental scientist, most of that time in the field—surveying water quality in rivers across the Southwest, training younger researchers, moving through the world with the quiet competence of a man who had built his life on observation and precision. His wife, Amira, had always said that his steadiness was what drew her to him. Even now, after forty-three years of marriage, she spoke of how he could sit for hours watching the smallest shifts in light on water, patient and present in a way that made her feel safe.

On a Tuesday in March, Khalil and his colleague Derek were conducting a routine assessment at a municipal treatment facility. They had done this work hundreds of times. Derek was younger—forty-five, energetic, always talking. They were checking the filtration system in the main chamber, a space Khalil knew intimately from three decades of visits. Khalil was showing Derek a valve mechanism when Derek lost his footing on the wet platform. In the instant before it happened, Khalil reached out. His hand caught Derek's arm, but the momentum was too great, and Khalil's own balance shifted. Derek fell backward, his head striking the concrete edge of the basin with a sound that Khalil would spend the rest of his life trying not to hear. Derek had survived, but barely—a traumatic brain injury, months in intensive care, a future that remained uncertain.

The guilt had been absolute and suffocating. But what surprised Khalil, in the weeks that followed, was how his mind had fractured the memory itself. He could recall the facts: Derek's fall, the sound, the ambulance, the hospital waiting room where Amira had found him sitting in complete silence. But when he tried to speak about it, the words would scatter. He knew what had happened—he could see it, almost—but the knowledge and the language had become separated, as though his mind had locked the narrative away in a place his tongue could not reach. With his therapist, with Amira, even alone in the dark, he would begin to explain and then simply stop, his mouth opening and closing on nothing. It was maddening, this inability to make the story coherent. It was as if what had occurred was too extreme, too aberrant from the life he had lived, to be fully real—a thing that belonged to someone else's story, not his.

Then came the triggers, and with them, the memories would surge back whole and unbearable. A sound—a sudden intake of breath, someone breathing heavily after climbing stairs—would snap him into that moment on the platform with such immediacy that he could not remember how to move. When Amira came home from the grocery store one evening and pulled him into a hug, her arms around his shoulders, his body had gone rigid. The physical affection that had always grounded him now propelled him backward into the accident, and he had pulled away from her without explanation, leaving her confused and hurt. Worst of all were the moments when he felt something close to happiness—when he was absorbed in reading, or when Amira made him laugh at something small—because the moment he recognized the feeling, the guilt would crash in and the memory would follow, intrusive and vivid, as if his mind was punishing him for any moment of peace. He had come to believe that happiness itself was dangerous, a kind of betrayal of Derek, and so he had begun to withdraw from the things that might bring it: his books, his wife's affection, the quiet satisfaction of his work. The memory was not something he experienced in isolation; it was always triggered by these small, ordinary moments, and when it came, it came with the overwhelming conviction that it was happening again, that Derek was falling again, that he was failing again.

Khalil had finally called a therapist after Amira found him one morning unable to get out of bed, paralyzed not by physical pain but by the weight of a memory he could not speak and could not escape. He was afraid that he was losing himself—that the man Amira had married, steady and present, was being erased by this thing he could not name or control. What he hoped for most was simply to be able to tell the story, to find the words that seemed to have been stolen from him, and to live in a world where a breath or a touch did not send him spiraling back to the worst moment of his life.
